extracted.intended_audience: researchers and conference organizers working on reviewer-assignment / similarity-computation algorithms (computer science / machine learning)
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, collecting data for, and evaluating algorithms that compute similarity/expertise scores between reviewers and papers to inform reviewer assignment in conferences. Covers dataset collection, evaluation metrics, algorithm inputs, and experimental protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold standard dataset desiderata (D1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dataset should comprise evaluations of expertise for papers participants read to a reasonable extent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect self-evaluations only for papers the participant actually read to a reasonable extent so the expertise judgments are informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold standard dataset desiderata (D2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dataset should be released publicly without disclosing any sensitive information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Release data in a form that preserves participants' privacy (e.g., do not release email addresses) while providing representations (Semantic Scholar IDs, metadata, PDF links) sufficient for algorithmic work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold standard dataset desiderata (D3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The dataset should comprise experts’ ratings of their own expertise rather than people judging other peoples’ expertise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-reported expertise (ex-post evaluations) rather than external judgments or ex-ante bids to better capture reviewers' true ability to judge a paper's content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant screening criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Prospective participants must have at least one paper published in the broad area of computer science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this screening to ensure contributors are qualified reviewers for the target domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper selection constraints for survey responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers reported by a participant should not be authored by them, and should be freely available online.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend arXiv or other open sources to ensure PDFs and metadata can be shared; this enables use of full texts where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Survey coverage and diversity recommendations
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask participants to recall 5–10 papers they read in the last year and provide expertise ratings; encourage selecting papers across the spectrum of expertise (some well-separated, some nearly tied), avoid ties, include less-famous papers, and include papers that may be tricky for algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide explicit instructions and examples (e.g., naive similarity pitfalls). Request at least 5 papers; recommended time 5–10 minutes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expertise rating scale and granularity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a 1 ('I am not qualified to review this paper') to 5 ('I have background necessary to evaluate all the aspects of the paper') scale with 0.25 step size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smaller step sizes help participants avoid ties and express fine-grained differences in expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data fields to release for participants and papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Participant: Semantic Scholar ID and complete bibliography (crawled). Paper: Semantic Scholar ID, title, abstract, list of authors, publication year, arXiv identifier, and links to freely available PDFs when available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Release these non-sensitive identifiers to enable reproducible algorithm development while withholding email addresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary evaluation metric — weighted Kendall’s Tau / normalized pairwise loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Define algorithm loss by penalizing incorrect pairwise orderings between two papers for the same reviewer by the absolute difference in the reviewer’s expertise; ties in algorithm scores incur half the penalty. Normalize the sum across participants relative to the worst-case (reverse ordering) to obtain L ∈ [0,1]; lower is better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This metric captures difficulty (smaller expertise differences are harder) by weighting errors by |ε_i - ε_j|; use this as main metric for ranking algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional ranking/evaluation metrics (WKTD@k, MRR@k, NDCG@k, Precision@k)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate algorithms using top-k variants: Weighted Kendall Tau Distance@k (WKTD@k), Mean Reciprocal Rank@k (MRR@k), Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain@k (NDCG@k), and Precision@k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define these metrics per participant (e.g., top-k sets Rk and Ak), aggregate across participants, and normalize WKTD appropriately; use multiple metrics to provide complementary views (lower WKTD is better; higher MRR/NDCG/Precision better).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper representation choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity-computation algorithms may operate on different representations of papers: (i) title only, (ii) title + abstract, (iii) full text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Title+abstract is often used and supported across algorithms; note that some algorithms (TF-IDF/TPMS) can use full text and that using full text can change relative performance (TPMS with full text can match Specter2 using titles+abstracts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer profile construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct reviewer profiles by selecting a set of reviewer papers (authors' past papers); authors used the 20 most recent papers from Semantic Scholar (use all if fewer than 20), ordered by publication year with uniform random tie-breaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Profile size choice affects available information; match realistic profile sizes (NeurIPS mean length ~16.5). Repeat stochastic profile construction multiple times (they repeat 10) and average to reduce randomness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pooling methods for aggregating paper-to-paper similarities
rubrics_metrics.description: Aggregate similarity scores between the submitted paper and each paper in a reviewer’s profile via pooling methods: max, mean, or percentile (e.g., 75th percentile).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Max can be sensitive to fraudulent/outlier papers; percentile pooling (75th) proposed to improve robustness against manipulation; evaluate multiple pooling strategies (the paper evaluates all three for Specter2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm baseline and families to evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a trivial baseline (constant score), TF-IDF/TPMS-style methods, OpenReview deep embeddings (ELMo, Specter, Specter+MFR, Specter2), ACL-trained similarity, and off-the-shelf LLMs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a broad set of algorithm families under comparable inputs and default parameters to assess relative strengths; note dataset-domain shifts (e.g., ACL-trained model trained on ACL abstracts may experience distribution shift).

rubrics_metrics.name: IDF corpus selection for TF-IDF / TPMS
rubrics_metrics.description: When using TF-IDF-based methods, choose the corpus used to compute IDF (authors used reviewers’ profiles plus reported papers; larger corpora like all submissions could improve IDF estimates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting an appropriate IDF corpus affects TF-IDF performance; document and justify IDF corpus choice when benchmarking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical estimation and confidence intervals
rubrics_metrics.description: Quantify uncertainty by bootstrapping participants (sample participants with replacement) to compute 95% confidence intervals over loss and over differences between algorithms; also average over repetitions of profile-construction randomness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use many bootstrap iterations (they use 1,000) and reuse constructed profiles if profile-construction randomness is negligible to save compute; also compute CIs for pairwise algorithm performance differences (e.g., relative to TPMS).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment-quality objectives beyond cumulative similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternative objectives for the assignment stage include cumulative similarity (sum of similarity scores), fairness (avoid discriminating against some submissions), envy-freeness, resistance to strategic behavior, and encouraging diversity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While this paper focuses on similarity computation, designers of assignment algorithms should consider these objectives—cumulative sum maximization may concentrate expertise unevenly; fairness and other notions address balanced assignment and robustness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling evaluation instances of varying difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Stratify evaluation into easy vs hard instances (e.g., pairs with large vs small expertise differences) and report performance separately because algorithms perform differently across difficulty levels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report error rates in both regimes (authors report 12%-30% in easy cases and 36%-43% in hard cases) to expose weaknesses that are masked by aggregate metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: LLM evaluation protocol (prompt & score format)
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating off-the-shelf LLMs, prompt them as an expert assigning an integer score (0–100) for reviewer-paper match; request a brief explanation and instruct to not hallucinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide the reviewer papers (titles+abstracts) and the new paper; require outputs in a strict format (<score> Explanation: ...). Ensure instructions emphasize grounding in provided inputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Known dataset limitations and recommended usage cautions
rubrics_metrics.description: Dataset size is limited (477 evaluations from 58 researchers) and has demographic/geographic skew (e.g., 74% participants from the US); most papers are recent (75% from 2020 or later) and 99% are in broad area of computer science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Users should be aware of these limitations when drawing conclusions; the authors encourage further contributions to increase size and diversity.
